items.title: China Is Back? I Tested Qwen 4 Max & It's Interesting..
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I review Alibaba's Qwen 4 Max Preview, explain its OpenCode setup on the Alibaba Token Plan, and test it on all six KingBench 4 apps. I show what it built, where it broke, and why its testing habits left serious bugs behind despite a total score of 30.6 out of 60 and a rank of 11 out of 14 models. I then show my PandaCode team demo, where a reviewer caught a flaw despite passing tests, before breaking down Token Plan pricing and its catches. Finally, I look at whether Chinese models have caught up and explain why I call this a decent preview, but not a new leader.

--
Key Takeaways:

🔍 Qwen 4 Max Preview launched without a benchmark table, open weights, or an API price, and access is through the Token Plan.
💻 OpenCode setup requires the QwenCloud provider block because the built-in model list does not yet include the preview.
📊 Qwen scored 30.6 out of 60 on KingBench 4, ranking 11
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi, welcome to another video. So Alibaba has launched Qwen 4 Max. Well, a preview of it. It came out on November 11th and it is a strange launch because there is no benchmark table, no open weights, and no API price. You can only use it through their token plan subscription and the preview ends on November 25. That also means none of the independent leaderboards have it yet. So if you want to know how good this model is, somebody has to actually test it. I ran it through Open Code on all six King Bench 4 apps and today I'll show you what it built, where it broke, how it behaves while it works, what the token plan is worth, and whether Chinese models are really catching up. First, the basics. Alibaba calls it their next flagship for coding and agentic work. It has a 1 million token context window. It takes text, images, and video as input and thinking is on by default. To use it, you need the token plan. It has four tiers, which are $6, $10, $18, and $4 a month, and each tier gives you a monthly pool of credits. I'll come back to what those credits actually buy. Setting it up in Open Code takes about 2 minutes. You run / connect, pick Alibaba token plan, and paste your key. The built-in model list does not have the new model yet, so you also add the Qwen cloud provider block from Alibaba's Open Code guide to your config and then you run / models and pick Qwen 4 Max preview. One thing to know is that Open Code limits this model to 32,000 output tokens by default. So I raised that limit before the run. Now the benchmark. King Bench 4 is six apps and each one gets a single prompt with no follow-ups. The apps are a Game Boy DS and 3DS emulator, a Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a keyboard configurator like Via, the first chapter of Pokémon Red, and a Fitbit desktop app. Independent evaluators then score each app out of 10 with a strict rubric. I ran Qwen at max effort on Open Code 2.2.7 which is a newer open code than my older runs used. So keep that in mind when I compare. Let' start with the emulator because this is the worst result. It scored 1.6 out of 10. The prompt asks for three consoles and Quen built one. If you open a DS or a 3DS file, it prints the header and tells you that emulation is not implemented. To be fair, it says this clearly in its final message, but two-thirds of the tasks are just missing. The Game Boy part is better than the score suggests. The CPU passes all 11 instruction tests and one of the classic rendering tests comes out pixel perfect, but the controls are swapped. The arrow keys act as A, B, start and select and the buttons act as the D-pad. Its own test checks the same wrong mapping, so the test passes and that pattern is going to come back. The second app is the Docker alternative and it scored three out of 10. It wrote a runtime called Vessel in plain Go with no dependencies. It pulls real images from Docker Hub and on Linux the isolation is real with separate namespaces and memory limits that actually kill a container. So why only a three? Because a crafted image can write files outside the image store on your actual disk as soon as you load it. My rubric caps any runtime with an escape like that at three, no matter what else works. Without the cap, this would have been a 5.3. Most models land on that same cap in this task. So Quen is not worse than the others here, but it is not safer either. The third app is the Room Designer and this is its best one at 7.7. You get a furnished room. You can place and drag furniture, rotate it, change the colors and the lamps really tint the room. The night preset looks good. The bugs are small but easy to find. If you type 12 into the width box, it applies the one first. The room shrinks to 2 m and half the furniture jumps to the middle and a sofa that is bigger than the room just pokes through the walls. A a 7.7 sounds fine, but six other models score above eight on this task. The fourth app is the Keyboard Configurator with 6.7. This is where Quen surprised me. Before it wrote any code, it spent about 30 steps reading the actual VA and QMK sources, and it shows the macros it stores on the keyboard match QMK's encoding byte for byte, and keymap edits, lighting, and the key tester all work. Only Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 scored higher than this. The main bug is a bad one, though. If the keyboard sends back a short reply, the app fills the gap with zeros and accepts it, and one edit followed by an undo then wiped 13 keys. The fifth app is Pokémon Red with 4.9, and this one hurts because the game is almost there. You can play from your bedroom to Brock, win the fight, and get the Boulder Badge, but the start menu never opens. One line reads the wrong variable name, so there is no save, no bag, and no party screen for the whole chapter. And if you lose to Brock, he never fights you again, so that run is dead. QN's final message says the full quest was verified end-to-end. It was not. Its test teleports between the story stages and hands itself a level 50 Charizard. The last app is the Fitbit desktop app, which got 6.7. It is a real native window. It starts in about a second. It looks polished, and the recovery and strain numbers are calculated correctly. The problem is your own data. There is no way to import a Fitbit export. Missing days show up as zero steps instead of no data, and sleep debt keeps growing and never clears. The worst one is a security bug. While the app is running, any website that is open in your browser can wipe your sync data. So the total is 30.6 out of 60, which is 51%. That puts QN 4 Max at rank 11 of the 14 models I have tested. Fable 5.2 leads with 42, Opus 5.5 has 34.7, and Kimi K3.1 Pro has 32.2. It even lands a little below DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which has 31 and costs 30 cents for a million input tokens. Now the scores only tell you half of it. So let's talk about how this model behaves because it has a very clear personality. The first trait is that it does not stop early. Every app took between 56 and 99 minutes, about 700 steps in total, and every run ended with a final builder test. is good to see. second trait is that it writes the whole first version before it compiles anything. The first build comes somewhere between step 20 and step 60. After that, it works in tight loops of build, test, and fix. The third trait is my favorite. It tests in the real thing. It drives a real browser, takes screenshots, and then actually looks at them. In the room designer, it saw that the evening preset rendered black, traced it through the render chain, and found a reversed function that produced an invalid number. It also spent 29 steps on a single container bug until it found the real cause. It is also very quiet. You get about one short sentence per step while the hidden thinking is around 25 times longer than the visible text. And every final message has a section about honest limits, which I like a lot. But there are two bad habits. When a test fails, it sometimes decides that the test is wrong and changes the test. Sometimes that is correct, and sometimes is how a bug survives. And it says verified for things it never saw. It said the Fitbit window was verified, but screen capture was blocked, so it never saw that window. If you put this together, you get the pattern of the whole run. Quinn tests a lot, but it tests its own understanding of the task. The swapped controls, the dead start menu, and the teleporting quest test are all bugs that its own tests could not see. And that is exactly why I would not run it alone, which brings me to Panda Code. Panda Code is my app for running coding agents as a team, and it can use open code as a harness. So I picked open code, selected Q and 4 Max preview, and turned on team mode. I gave it a small task on a demo repo. The architect wrote a plan with three assignments. One worker built the feature, a second one wrote the tests in parallel, and a third one reviewed the result. All three ran on Q and 4 Max. The tests passed 34 out of 33 and the reviewer still caught a real flaw because the tests had locked the wrong behavior in as correct. That is the same habit we saw in the benchmark and a second pair of eyes is what catches it. All of it runs on the same token plan. Now, what is the token plan worth? The four tiers give you 20,000 45,000 80,000 and 200,000 credits a month. Two days before this launch, Alibaba raised the credits on every tier and cut the top tier from $68 to $43. During the preview, QN four max also uses only about 20% of the normal credit rate and 8% at night China time. The whole benchmark with the three reruns came to about 104 million tokens and I did not hit a single rate limit or quota error. Most of those tokens are cash reads, but that is still six full apps. I ran all six at the same time and Alibaba lists six to eight agents at once only on the $43 tier while the 10 tier tier lists two to three which is enough for one person in one editor. The same plan also includes QN 3.8 GLM 5.3 and the DeepSeek V4 models. For comparison, Alibaba's older coding plan was $50 a month and it does not include this model. There are catches. Alibaba does not publish how many credits a request costs and you can only see your usage in their console, so you cannot plan it in advance. The plan is sold in the Singapore region only. The individual plan cannot be canceled and the terms say it is for interactive use in coding tools and not for automation scripts. And this model is retired on November 25, so you are buying the plan for whatever comes after it. I think the $10 tier is a low risk way to try all of this, but I would not pay for the top tier just for a two week preview. Finally, the big question, are Chinese models catching up? On the artificial analysis index, the best American model Fable 5.2 scores 65 and the best Chinese model Kimi K 3.1 Pro scores 46. That is a gap of 19 points, but only four days before that index was updated, Kimi was fourth overall on the old version, so the gap depends a lot on who measures it and when. My own bench says something similar. Kimi is only 2.5 points behind Opus 5.5 out of 60, but it is almost 10 points behind Fable. So I think the best Chinese models have caught up with the pack. While GLM and MiniMax are still behind it, none of them has caught up with the leader, and every time they get close, the leader moves. Where they clearly win is price. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash costs 30 cents for a million input tokens, while Fable costs $8 and on my bench, DeepSeek gets about three quarters of Fable's score. Qwen For Max does not change this picture. It did not beat Kimi or DeepSeek Flash on my tests, and it launched closed with no weights and no numbers. I'm saying this about a preview, so the final model could be better, but today it is a mid-table model with a very cheap way to use it. So should you use it? If you already have a token plan, yes, try it, especially for protocol heavy work and desktop apps where it placed third and fourth on my bench because it does its research and it tests hard. Just keep a reviewer on top of it and do not trust the word verified. If you want the best model for one-shot builds, this is not it. Overall, it's a decent preview, but not a new leader. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option [music] or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
